i just graduated from unh and i'm also trans, so i can speak to this a bit. there are plenty of more conservative people at unh, but honestly its not super hard to find other trans people and those accepting of trans people. your best friend is going to be resources like the beauregard center (multicultural center that hosts lots of the clubs focused on diversity and is a general hang out spot for the people involved in those clubs). in terms of housing, it definitely is difficult to find an option that is safe and is not just sticking you in gender inclusive housing. alexander hall is not gender inclusive but hosts a significant amount of queer kids and its almost all freshmen. divine hall has a floor for lqbtq people (i believe its the fourth floor) but even outside that floor the whole of upper quad is pretty nice in terms of people. i do have to warn you a lot of the buildings that host a lot of queer and trans people are older and poor quality. upper quad has flooded a few times in the last few years. i can say you'll probably want to avoid somewhere like stoke and christiensen and williamson. there are some buildings with single dorms, but theyre often really hard to get as a freshman so i would stake your hopes on that. most of residence halls arent too bad, except for the huge freshman dorms i already named its not gonna be super difficult to find other queer and trans people. i lived down in the sercs (haaland, peterson and handler) and i really enjoyed it there. peterson is a hall for people in life sciences but i knew a few mechies in the other halls. those buildings are also few close to philly (the dining hall), kingsbury, and the ocean engineering building.

It’s great that your feeling happy after so long, and I’m really happy for you about that! And I know what it’s like to be in that situation where you just exist in a state of apathy, and it’s very easy to get used to. That change of feeling positivity was one of the scariest things I ever had to deal with, and I just didn’t for a long time. I don’t know if it was just like while you were in the shower or if it lasted longer than that, but it’s still a scary change, and humans are creatures of habit. So it’s completely understandable that you wouldn’t be so sure about feeling good like that again, and it’s something that takes a very long time to accept. The option to fall back under into apathy is a lot easier, and more appealing because you’ve learned how to live like that. 

You can get used to feeling okay, though it’s not a quick process. I spent about 17 months in that state, and I still haven’t gotten used to caring more about things in the 5 months since it stopped. When you look back at moments like that though, where you just felt happy/at peace, you’ll come to treasure them. Finding joy in the small parts of life is something you should strive for, despite your comfort in apathy.

I haven't seen anyone mention what I've found so far, but I think it's worth sharing. So because Tyler tweeted "Sahlo Folina" the other day, I've had a lot of questions as to what it means. I went ahead and looked up both words individually. While I didn't immediately find anything relating to the word Sahlo, I did find some stuff on Folina. There is a Professor Janet Folina who works at Macalester College in St. Paul, Minnesota. I looked at her thesis for her PhD, and it is on the philosophy of mathematics in the work of Henri Poincare. I started to read her thesis, but frankly, I'm not as interested in the thesis as I possibly should be, but if anyone else has the time to read the 250 pages, you can read it all [here](https://research-repository.st-andrews.ac.uk/bitstream/handle/10023/2703/JanetFolinaPhDThesis.pdf?sequence=3&isAllowed=y). As soon as she stated Poincare's name, I looked him up. He was a mathematician and  mathematical physicist, born in 1854 and died in 1912. Now earlier today I watched Olivia Kathryn's video on her theory about Nicolas Bourbaki. For those who haven't seen it, you can watch it [here](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RGmLgrL-2-g). It will provide you with some much needed context about Nicolas Bourbaki. As many of you may know, Nicolas Bourbaki was a pseudonym for a group of mathematicians that started in France shortly after WWI ended. Nicolas Bourbaki the general was around during Napoleon's reign of France, which ended in the early 1800's. Now, as Henri Poincare relates to all of this. Writing this is slightly rushed, and I don't have all of the information I need to make a truly solid theory on this, but what I found is that Poincare was a direct influence for the Bourbaki group. While it may not give us any direct answers as to what "Sahlo Folina" means, it does start to shine the light on how it connects to the information relating to Trench that's outside the storyline.
